It improves overall image compositing performance by up to 40% compared to separated rendering and compositing phases [S1, unofficial].

The claim states that the approach improves overall image compositing performance by up to 40% compared to separated rendering and compositing phases. The evidence in Source [S1] explicitly states: 'According to our tests and others [14, 17], overlapping the ray casting and compositing can improve the overall image compositing performance by as much as 40%.' The text further clarifies that the 'overlapping' approach (sending segments during rendering) is contrasted with the 'first approach' where 'local rendering [is] completely [separated] from the global compositing' (sending large messages after local ray-tracing finishes). Thus, the evidence directly supports the claim.
supported
- **When to Use:** When network bandwidth is a bottleneck and data partitioning results in irregular ray segment distributions [S1, unofficial].

The evidence explicitly states that 'irregular shapes and data partitioning cause rays to enter/exit multiple faces and create varying numbers of local ray segments, leading to variable ray buffer sizes' and that 'unstructured domain tends to be irregular in shape... Consequently, the ray segments which contribute to an individual pixel cannot be combined until they are all received'. It also identifies 'network congestion' as a problem with the non-overlapping approach (sending large messages at once) and proposes the overlapping approach (sending smaller messages throughout) to 'reduce network congestion'. Therefore, the claim that the overlapping strategy is used when bandwidth is a bottleneck and data partitioning causes irregular distributions is fully supported by the text.
